1:
Henry reports that some attach the opening words to the close of the previous chapter and read them with its promises, so that once the people have appointed a head and centred in him they may say this to one another with triumph, calling each other by the names of mercy again and no longer lying under the doom of the negatives. He extends it to a spiritual Israel made up of Jews and Gentiles without distinction, who own one another for the people of God and stir one another up both to give thanks for their common salvation and to walk worthy of it. Calvin makes the same connection but presses the order of it: the prophet had first spoken of a public proclamation, since it is not in men's power to make themselves the children of God but God freely adopts them, and the mutual exhortation follows that proclamation rather than preceding it. Wesley adds the condition, that they are still within the covenant of their father Abraham if they will walk with God as he did. Ellicott notes the grammatical signal, that the two names appearing here without the negative prefix show the awakening of conscience has given them their privileges back.

Who the mother is proves less settled than it looks. Ellicott takes her for the nation Israel viewed as a collective abstract, with the children as the individual inhabitants who make up that aggregate. Gill agrees that she is the body of the nation and reads the plea itself christologically, as laying before her the sin of rejecting the Messiah, reproving her for it and showing her the danger of persisting, as the apostles did. Clarke names the city twice and does not name the same one: introducing the chapter he calls the mother Samaria, whose captivity is threatened for forsaking God and ascribing her prosperity to idols, while at the second verse he addresses the people of Judah and calls the mother Jerusalem.

Keil and Delitzsch stand apart from all of them on what the restoration means. The patriarchal promise of an innumerable multiplication is to be realized, they argue, through the pardon and restoration of Israel as the nation of the living God, and that shows plainly that we are not to look for the fulfilment in a return of the ten tribes from captivity to their native land — quite apart from the fact that the historical books mention the return only of a portion of two tribes.

The threat of stripping draws three different explanations. Gill takes the day of birth for the nativity of the people in Egypt, when they were in bondage without wealth or possessions or a country of their own, and reads the sentence as a warning that this should be their case again. Ellicott gives the same historical reference and then adds a darker possibility, that the words allude to the custom of female infanticide, which he says still prevails widely in the East as it did in the ancient world, the child being simply abandoned to death on the day she was born. Clarke looks instead to the penalty for adultery, and reports the practice of the ancient Germans, who shaved off the offender's hair, stripped her naked before her relatives and in that state drove her from her husband's house; and he adds a judgment of his own on such punishments, that however reproachful they were to the delinquent they had no tendency to promote her moral reformation. Keil and Delitzsch note that the following verse depends in sense on the same word lest, though in form it stands as an independent sentence.
4:
Calvin heads off a reading he thinks the words invite and do not bear. It was far from the prophet's mind, he insists, to teach the faithful who had already repented that they ought to condemn their own mother; nothing of the kind is meant. What the passage does is check the waywardness of a people who never ceased contending with God as though he had been more severe than just toward them, and Calvin notes that the Lord now comes close to each individual after having spoken generally of the whole nation.

What makes the children children of whoredoms is variously explained. Clarke takes it of consecration: they are all idolaters and have been dedicated to idols, whose marks they bear. Ellicott presses the family likeness instead — the children are like their mother, not only born of doubtful parentage but personally defiled — and turns it into a charge against the whole society, since idolatry is enshrined not merely in the national sanctuary and the royal palace but in the affections of a people who love to have it so and who endorse their mother's degradation. Gill carries the reference forward, applying it to the posterity of the Jews in succeeding ages until their conversion comes, persisting in the sins of their forefathers and in the rejection of the Messiah.

Two of them notice the awkward shift of person in the next verse, where the address changes from your mother to their mother. Ellicott reports a rendering that would begin the clause with yea rather than for, which he says would account for the change more easily, while granting that such shifts are very frequent in Hebrew prophecy; Keil and Delitzsch reach the same observation through the pronominal suffixes attached to the words for mother and for her that bare them. Gill takes the clause either as the reason for what precedes, why she is to be pleaded with and not owned as a wife, or else as joined to what follows.

On the lovers themselves Ellicott is the most exact. The word is used in a bad sense, and the aggravation of her shame lies in the direction of the pursuit — she seeks them rather than being sought — while what she ascribes to them is precisely the set of temporal benefits that the history of the covenant shows to have come from another hand. Gill glosses the harlotry as idolatry outright, and makes it the reason for everything in the passage: why she is pleaded with, why she is not owned as a wife, why she is exhorted to put her whoredoms away, and why the evils threatened hang over her if she continues. Keil and Delitzsch set out the inventory she claims from her lovers — bread and water, wool and flax, oil and drink — as the very things named again later when they are taken from her. Clarke passes over the verse quickly, referring the reader to another prophet in whom nearly the same words occur and are discussed at length.
6:
Henry frames the threat by its purpose. God warns that he may not wound, and threatens that he may not strike; if a people do not turn he will whet his sword, and if they turn he will sheathe it. They did not turn, and therefore all this came upon them, the earlier threatening showing that what followed was the execution of a divine sentence for their wickedness and is written for our admonition. Henry adds an observation about the shape of these particular verses: a promise is annexed to the threatening, that the distress should be the means of convincing them of their folly and bringing them home to their duty, so that good is brought out of evil; and since that is the effect, it is hard to say whether the prediction, or the distress itself, should be called a threatening or a promise.

Calvin explains the necessity rather than the purpose. Chastisement is needed when people congratulate themselves in their vices, and when God sees that men do not immediately confess their sins he defends his own cause like one pleading before a judge; here he shows that he could not do otherwise than punish so great an obstinacy, since no other remedy appeared.

The hedge of thorns is read three ways, and the difference is one of scope. Gill offers the two agricultural senses and prefers the second: fields are fenced with thorns to keep beasts out, or rather closes are fenced to keep cattle in from straying, and he takes the figure for afflictions and particularly for wars that would stop them stirring from place to place — specifically from going to the shrines of the calves, or from going down to the Egyptians. Keil and Delitzsch make the hedge and the wall together denote a transportation into a situation where she could no longer continue her adultery with the idols at all. Clarke extends it furthest: it is a matter of putting the judgments beyond escape, of bringing them into circumstances in which the pursuit of their expensive idolatry becomes impossible, and finally of leading her so deep into captivity that she never finds the road back to her own land.

Gill draws a small but exact inference from the next verse. Since she has been hedged in and walled up, she cannot in any proper sense go after her lovers at all; so the following after them must be understood of her affections and desires, pursuing them with the eagerness of men bent on what they want, rather than of any actual journey. Keil and Delitzsch set the sequence out in its order — she follows and does not overtake, seeks and does not find, and only then says that she will return to her first husband because it was better with her then than now — and they carry it straight on into the reason given afterwards, that she did not know who it was that gave her the corn and wine and oil, and multiplied the silver and gold which were spent on an idol.
8:
Calvin finds two distinct sins in the ignorance charged here. The superstitious offend in two ways: first they ascribe to their idols what belongs to God alone, and then they rob God of his own honour, since they do not understand that he is the only giver of all things and reckon their labour lost if they were to worship him. In the Israelites this was an inexcusable stupidity, Calvin says, because they had been abundantly taught that everything supporting human life flows from God's bounty, having the clear testimony of Moses and the land itself as a living demonstration. Gill presses the same point as culpability rather than accident: the ignorance was wilful and affected and therefore blameable, since she might have known but would not, and did not set her mind to know. Clarke turns it into two general observations, how often the gifts of God's immediate bounty are attributed to fortuitous causes, and how often they are perverted into means of dishonouring him, since God gives wisdom, strength and property and men use them to sin against him with the greater skill, power and effect.

Ellicott alone changes the tense, rendering it that she knows not that it is I who gave, and finds in the clause something more than a charge. This yearning of the Lord over the results of his own chastisements he calls a wonderful anticipation of the parable of the son who came to himself in a far country. He also identifies the produce named as the chief indigenous crops of the land, distinguishing them from the gold that was imported from abroad.

Who the lovers are is not settled among them. Clarke makes them her idols together with her allies, faithful or faithless. Ellicott names the historical agency by which the goods were taken back, the Assyrian king and the year of his coming. Gill reports the Targum's rendering of them as the people and the common identification with Egyptians and Assyrians, inclines himself toward the Romans whom the Jews courted as friends, and then judges it best to take the whole more generally, of the folly of rejecting the Messiah being made manifest by the punishment that followed. Keil and Delitzsch leave the persons aside and work on the word for what is uncovered, a term occurring nowhere else, which they derive from a root meaning to be withered or faded and take, following another commentator, for a body that has suffered much defilement, noting that the Greek version renders it freely by a word for uncleanness.

The ceasing of the mirth draws a defence of the mirth itself from Ellicott. The rejoicing is indicative of the general character of the ceremonial and is certainly not in itself a bad sign, he argues, since David danced before the Lord and justified the act, and no one was to appear before God with a sad countenance any more than before an earthly ruler; he also distinguishes the feast days from the solemn feasts, the second term being the more generic in Hebrew while the first denoted the three great festivals. Calvin describes the same loss as a stripping of the whole external pomp which was among them the guise of religion, and takes the joy meant to be sacred joy, suggesting that the word may refer to the dancing customary on their festal days. Clarke states the cause plainly, that the city would be pillaged and destroyed and so her joyous assemblies and religious feasts must cease.
12:
The vines and fig trees are taken by all of them as standing for more than themselves. Gill says they are singled out as the most fruitful and beneficial growths of the land, and gives the fulfilment concretely from the historian: when Judea was overrun, timber was felled to build forts and cast up mounts against the city, so that ground once adorned with orchards and gardens was left miserable to look upon. Ellicott prefers make desolate to destroy, observes that these two trees are the standing emblems of secure possession and quiet, and allows that the ruin might come either by fire or by drought. He adds a textual note, that the Greek translators read a different word in the following clause and rendered it make them a testimony instead of make them a forest, though he judges the received text yields the more vivid picture. Wesley identifies what is laid waste as the vineyards and olive yards together with the plots where fruit trees had been set.

What she called her wages is where Clarke and Wesley meet. Clarke says the people credited every benefit of providence to the images they served, treating it as hire received from them; Wesley puts it that they gave the praise of all their plenty elsewhere. Keil and Delitzsch tie the clause back to the festivals just abolished, since it is by removing the produce that gladdens a man's heart that the Lord brings the festal rejoicing to an end.

The plural in the days of Baalim divides them, and the division is substantive. Clarke reads it as a multitude of separate deities: Baal served as the general title for a male divinity, as Astarte did for a female, so that one plural gathers up all the male objects of worship and the other all the female, particular kinds being distinguished by an epithet attached to the title. Wesley says much the same, that the great image of the ten tribes gave its title to the whole crowd of divinities they served. Ellicott construes the plural quite otherwise, as the cult of a single divinity carried on at many sanctuaries with distinguishing local features, so that the several compound titles denote local forms of one god rather than a pantheon; and on that footing he glosses the phrase as covering the entire era through which a faithless Israel practised that cult.

Gill reads the days as those of the forefathers and the reckoning as punishment for their idolatries, adding a scruple about the generation actually punished: they did not themselves serve those particular divinities, but had raised up other lords and lusts and images of their own within the heart. Clarke defines the terms one by one, that visiting signifies inflicting punishment and that the days stand for the acts of false worship committed on them. Calvin uses the verse to press again what he takes to be the necessary warning of the passage: that when God deals harshly with men he is reckoning with their sins and inflicting a just penalty, since people may know themselves chastised and still fail to search and examine themselves as they ought; and he remarks that the prophet points as with a finger to what chiefly offended God in Israel, namely that worship itself had been corrupted among them.
14:
The little connective that opens the verse is worked over by four of them, and they do not agree what it does. Henry keeps its full causal force and treats the result as a wonder: the promises follow close on the threatenings and are actually joined to the declaration of sinfulness on which those threatenings rest, so that after she went after her lovers and forgot me comes therefore I will allure her — where one would have expected therefore I will abandon her and never look after her again. Ellicott denies the inference, saying the word does not make God's gentle treatment a consequence of Israel's sin; some prefer to render it nevertheless, but he takes it as a particle sometimes used to make a strong transition, linked with what precedes without drawing a conclusion from it. Gill reports the same alternative rendering from the lexicographers, notwithstanding or nevertheless, and paraphrases the sense accordingly, that although such methods had been used to no purpose God would now do what follows. Keil and Delitzsch settle it the same way, expressly rejecting the assuredly of some versions in favour of nevertheless.

Gill puts the change of method in the plainest terms: since the rough ways will not answer, another and more gentle way is taken, and instead of threatening and terrifying and punishing there will be alluring and persuading and enticing with loving words. Calvin adds that God would not merely become propitious at last but would make all their punishments conducive to their salvation and medicines to heal their diseases. He also notes an inversion in the clauses, so that the sense runs that God will persuade her after he has drawn her into the desert; and he pauses on the verb, which is often taken in a bad sense of deceiving or wheedling but here means to speak kindly, so that God persuades a rebellious and obstinate people to what is right.

Clarke draws the whole out as a domestic scene and says he takes it for the simple meaning of the metaphors. A very affectionate husband, dealing with an unfaithful wife, does not make her a public example but takes her in private, talks to her and reasons with her, puts her on her good behaviour and promises to pass by everything if she will amend; meanwhile he provides what she needs, and by opening a door of hope makes it possible for her to be fully reconciled and to rejoice as at the beginning when he first took her by the hand. Wesley compresses the same into two glosses, that the alluring is an inclining of her mind to consider what is proposed, and that the wilderness is deep distress.

Where the wilderness is meant to be found divides the historical readers. Ellicott makes the exile in Babylon a repetition of the wilderness experience in which she had first been espoused, and paraphrases the speaking to her heart as speaking comfortingly and lovingly. Keil and Delitzsch read the promise as the opening of a two-part movement, the conversion of the nation first and the renewal of the covenant mercies afterwards, and render the valley named here as the valley of tribulation turned into a door of hope. Clarke supplies the geography, that the valley was very fruitful and lay to the north of Jericho not far from Gilgal. Gill carries the promise forward past both, applying it to the call and conversion of a spiritual Israel of Jews and Gentiles in the first times of the gospel, as an apostle quotes it, and then to the withdrawal of the believing Jews from Jerusalem before its destruction, when they removed to Pella as the church historian relates.
15:
Where the blessing comes from is read three different ways, and the difference is between place and time. Gill offers both without deciding, either from the wilderness into which she has been brought or from the time of her being brought there and spoken to comfortably. Ellicott makes it a departure rather than a source, rendering it away from thence and taking the sense to be as soon as she has left the wilderness of exile and discipline. Wesley takes it purely temporally, from the time of their repentance. Gill treats the vineyards as standing for temporal blessings generally and as emblems of spiritual ones, so that from the moment God deals thus graciously he gives larger measures and continual supplies of grace.

The valley named as a door of hope draws opposite emphases. Ellicott stresses what it had been: a place associated with the disgrace and punishment that fell on Israel at her very entrance into the land, which in later days would be regarded instead as the threshold of a blessed life, its sorrowful associations illuminated with happy anticipation. Wesley stresses what it had been in the other direction, calling it a large, fruitful and pleasant valley near Jericho at the entrance of the land, which was a door of hope to Israel of old and will be such a door again to a repenting Israel. Keil and Delitzsch keep both senses in their rendering, giving the name as the valley of tribulation and setting it directly against the door of hope. Clarke passes over the valley here and fixes on the singing instead, taking it for the responsive song used on high festival occasions and at marriages, and noting that the Song of Solomon is a composition of that kind.

The change of names is agreed to be the heart of the promise, and the reason for it is agreed too, though stated differently. Clarke distinguishes the two words as titles of feeling: the one means my man or my husband and is a title of love and affection, the other means my master and excites fear and apprehension, and howsoever good that second title might be in itself it was now rendered improper by having been prostituted to false gods. Ellicott makes the same point historically, that a bride's husband was frequently called her lord, so that the word was unobjectionable in itself, but that as applied to God it was henceforth to be strictly avoided on account of its idolatrous associations. Wesley reads the calling as a whole disposition rather than a form of address, an owning of God as husband by words, affections and obedience together, and a delight in calling him so.

Calvin uses the verse to identify what repentance actually produces. The prophet expands his subject, he says, to show that when the people repented the fruits of repentance would openly appear; and the fruit he records is that they would then begin to worship God purely, all superstitions being abolished. The word husband is chosen, on Calvin's reading, to show the people that once corrected they would be mindful of the covenant God had made with them. Gill locates the whole in the gospel dispensation and its later times, at the conversion of the Jews and the bringing in of the fulness of the Gentiles, when God will persuade them to seek the Messiah and will speak comfortably to them.
17:
Keil and Delitzsch draw the two verses together by a single observation about cause. As soon as the nation ceases to call God by the name it had shared with the idols, the custom of taking the names of the Baals into its mouth ceases of itself; and they note that this too is here spoken of as God's own work rather than the people's achievement. Gill extends the removal of the names beyond Israel, reporting that it reaches the mouths of the converted Jews and even, as one rabbinic commentator allows, of the Gentiles, and adds the qualification that the names would not vanish from speech altogether but would be spoken only with detestation and abhorrence rather than with honour and affection. Wesley states it as an abolition of memory, the false gods perishing together with their names.

Calvin turns the promise of the following verse into a general doctrine about providence. The prophet shows that the people would be happy in every way once restored to favour, and at the same time reminds us that the cause of all evils is that men provoke God's wrath; for since God has all creatures at his will and in his hand, he can arm them in vengeance against us whenever he pleases, and when he is propitious he can make everything in heaven and earth conducive to our safety. Calvin points to the threatenings of the law, where God warns that when he purposes to punish he will make the brute animals and the birds and the creeping things execute his judgments.

Ellicott puts the same relation the other way about, as a correspondence: there shall be harmony without answering to the moral harmony within, the brute creation changing from hostility to man, and wars with foreign foes no longer desolating the borders. Clarke itemises what the covenant secures — an agreement with the birds, beasts and reptiles so that flocks are not destroyed nor crops spoiled, the prevention of every species of war with the calamities arising from it, and safety from robbers and nightly alarms. Gill is careful about the word covenant itself, taking it to mean that God promises this and that the promise shall be as sure and firm and as much to be depended on as if it had been settled by covenant, to be enjoyed as a covenant mercy and observed as strictly by the creatures.

When it is fulfilled is the one point at which they part. Keil and Delitzsch tie the peace directly to the abolition of idolatry and false religion, as the state the church attains once that is complete. Wesley divides the fulfilment in two, holding that the promise was made good in some measure to the Jews returning out of captivity while the full accomplishment belongs to the church of Christ. Gill and Ellicott leave the whole in the future, Gill within the latter-day scheme he has been following through the chapter and Ellicott as the outward counterpart of an inward change not yet made.
19:
The betrothal is understood by all four as a marriage relation formed rather than restored, but they differ on who is being married. Gill denies that the whole body of the elect is meant, since those were secretly betrothed in the everlasting covenant from eternity and this verse looks forward; he applies it instead to the Jews when converted in the latter day, at what he calls the marriage of the Lamb with them and with the fulness of the Gentiles. Clarke keeps the emblem the chapter has used throughout, the people considered as a wife unfaithful to her husband, and now betrothed afresh. Keil and Delitzsch render the repeated verb strictly as betrothing to oneself, and mark the threefold repetition as the structure of the promise.

What the accompanying words mean produces the sharpest disagreement of the tile. Clarke reads the four terms as so many measures of the transaction — righteousness according to law, reason and equity; judgment according to what is fit and becoming; lovingkindness as the utmost affection; and mercies as the forgiving and blotting out of all past miscarriages — and suggests besides that there may be an allusion here to the dowry given at a betrothal. Calvin reports and declines a more refined explanation. Some, he says, take righteousness for what is conferred on us by God through gratuitous imputation and judgment for the defence he affords against the violence and assaults of our enemies; but he doubts not that the prophet intimates something more general, namely that this covenant would stand firm because there would be truth and rectitude on both sides. Gill agrees with neither in emphasis, reading faithfulness in the following verse as the keeping of the marriage contract inviolable, and turning it into an argument about Christ: he will never suffer his faithfulness to fail nor break his covenant, being faithful to the Father who appointed him as he is to his people, and it is he who makes them faithful in return and gives them the faith by which they believe.

Calvin adds that the third clause confirms what he takes the whole to establish, the fixed and unchangeable duration of the marriage, and he appeals to another prophet's covenant language to make the point clear. Keil and Delitzsch let the promise run straight on into the knowledge that follows from it, so that being betrothed in faithfulness and knowing the Lord are set as one movement.

Clarke draws out the knowing at length and makes it the guarantee of everything else. There shall be no more infidelity on the one side nor divorce on the other, he says; the people shall experience God to be the sole and present and eternal good of their immortal spirit, and when that conviction is fully rooted there can be no more idolatry, since it will then be seen for what it is. On the negative side he glosses faithfulness as the end of prostituting herself to idols and a cleaving instead to the one who calls himself her husband. Gill reaches the same result by his own route, making the faithfulness first Christ's and only then, derivatively, the church's.
21:
The chain of hearing that runs down from heaven to the harvest is spelled out most fully by Clarke and Wesley. Clarke observes that the promise to hear is repeated in order to show how fully the thing was determined and how implicitly the promise might be depended on, and then takes the heavens for the visible sky and the atmosphere where the vapours are collected, so that God hears the clouds when they would deposit their fertilising showers, and the clouds in turn hear the earth when it seems to supplicate for them. Wesley makes God the first and universal cause who influences the heavens and commands their dew and showers, and describes a dry earth as crying to the heavens for refreshment while the seed sown and the vines and olives planted, being at a stand, cry to the earth for the kindly influences that will let them spring up and yield fruit. Gill sets the same abundance in his own frame, that when the espousals are made the whole creation will contribute of its riches and plenty to furnish a marriage feast; and at the next verse he has the corn and the vines and the olive trees requesting the earth to admit them and give them moisture, understanding by their fruit the graces of the Spirit communicated through word and ordinance.

Keil and Delitzsch keep the sequence bare, rendering the hearing as passing from God to heaven, from heaven to earth, and from earth to the corn and the new wine and the oil, and from these to the name with which the chapter closes.

On the sowing, three of them notice that the name itself is the pivot. Clarke says the promise alludes to the import of the name, which means the seed of God, so that in the sowing it appears that mercy has been shown to those who had not obtained mercy and the covenant renewed with those who were not a people. Calvin thinks the allusion has not been improperly noticed by others, and explains why the promise was needed at this point: a fruitful increase of corn and wine and oil had been promised, but to what end, unless the land had numerous inhabitants? So the prophet adds the increase of the people, setting God's new favour against the vengeance he had earlier pronounced when he said that though they were immense in number only a remnant should be preserved. Gill takes the sowing for the multiplication of a spiritual seed and offspring, and reports that two rabbinic commentators understood the words of Israel increasing and being fruitful.

Whether the promise has yet been fulfilled is where they finally divide. Ellicott points to the apostolic use of it, saying that Paul considers this great prediction truly fulfilled when, by the acceptance of the divine hope of Israel, both Jews and Gentiles are called the children of the living God. Wesley divides the fulfilment, observing that the Jews multiplied after the Babylonian captivity but that their numbers have increased much more since the preaching of the gospel. Gill places the whole in the latter day, at a conversion still to come of both Jews and Gentiles. Clarke, having laid out what the promise contains, ends by doubting that it has yet been accomplished at all.
